title: Justification: What Must I Do To Be Saved?
description: By Fr. Basil Cole, O.P., and Fr. John Baptist Ku, O.P. Caravaggio, “The Calling of Saints Peter and Andrew,” 1603, via Wikimedia Commons. The Question of Justification The question, “what must I do to be saved,” was posed by the rich young man in Matthew 19:16 (and Mark 10:17), as well as by the suicidal jailer in Acts 16:30. In reply, Jesus and Paul, respectively, do not say, “nothing, God will do it all.” Jesus says, “keep the commandments” and “go, sell what you possess . . . and come, follow me” (19:17, 21). And Paul says, “believe in the Lord Jesus.” But does that mean that I save myself, or that I at least meet God halfway? No. Earning eternal life is infinitely above the natural powers of man. But then, have I no part in my own salvation? At the Final Judgment, will God be judging himself since my actions are completely irrelevant to salvation? Even if I actually do evil things, if I have no free will to choose good versus evil, I will be like an irrational animal just following my instincts. And although we might be enraged at a fox that kills our chickens, we don’t blame the fox as if he were committing a sin. So, how should we understand our being rescued from sin and justified by God? Fortunately, St. Thomas Aquinas addresses this issue in question 113 of the first part of the second part of the Summa Theologiae. Aquinas divides the Summa Theologiae into three parts: (1) on God as he is in himself, (2) on rational creatures’ movement toward God, and (3) on Christ, man’s way back to God. The second part is itself divided into two parts: (1) on anthropology (man’s nature and end, and virtue in general) and (2) on specific virtues. At the end of the first section of the second part, Aquinas treats of grace, which was only implicit in the previous articles.

title: The Greatness of Humility
description: What is humility? Now humility makes a man a good subject to ordinance of all kinds and in all matters; while every other virtue has this effect in some special matter. Therefore after the theological virtues, after the intellectual virtues which regard the reason itself, and after justice, especially legal justice, humility stands before all others. ( ST.II-II.Q161.A5.C (emphasis added). To appreciate the greatness of humility, consider that humility stands before the cardinal virtues of temperance and fortitude . Does not their status as cardinal virtues make them greater than humility? Humility stands before magnanimity and magnificence . How can it be that lowly humility surpasses these virtues of greatness, one of which is even called the crown of the virtues? To answer why humility is so significant , we will first answer: what is humility? Humility is about aspiration for great things, and it has three main elements: a control element, knowledge element, and motivation element. Humility is the virtue by which we control our aspirations for anything we think makes us greater. Aquinas refers to these aspirations with the term hope. Sometimes we need to strengthen these aspirations, but we typically need to restrain them. This act of control is called moderation. We control aspirations in light of self-knowledge, in regards to especially our deficiencies and limitations. We control our aspirations out of divine reverence. We are motivated by divine reverence to act humbly, and this motivation guides us to seek our proper place in God’s providence. Let’s unpack humility’s greatness and these three elements and see why humility is so significant. Thanks for reading Investigations by the Thomistic Institute! title: The Soul of Goodness
description: Peter Vilhelm Ilsted, “A Mother and Child in an interior,” 1898, via Wikimedia Commons. The Difficulty of Virtue In his Nicomachean Ethics , in a sentence filled with insight, both anthropological and psychological, Aristotle observes, “Anyone can get angry, that is easy… but to be so with the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive, and in the right way, that is not for everyone, nor is it easy; wherefore goodness is both rare and laudable and noble.” 1 In effect, Aristotle is saying that human nature is wild and passionate, and that this natural wildness is essentially good inasmuch as it is an innate principle of actions that are themselves good, at least to the extent they can achieve goodness. However, he is also saying that our wild and passionate nature requires further formation if it is to become altogether good—“laudable and noble”—but that such formation in goodness, however dearly needed, is nevertheless terribly rare. It is so rare precisely because of the difficulty of bringing this formation to completion. This is in fact the principal positive difficulty of human life—the entirely natural challenge with which we are tasked as we proceed toward the future. It is the difficulty of receiving the gift of the goodness of our nature while simultaneously taking responsibility for the proper maturation of this nature—all so that our nature might attain its proper completion in our individual lives. This difficulty has a name; its name is virtue—for virtue is the immediate goal of this tough process of formation. Yet, while difficult, this task is most certainly worth the effort.
